context: long-span-roof-led · floor-trench power/AV rigging + smoke-control test drive the back end

brief.intro: New to this project type? An exhibition or convention centre is really one very large, column-free room (or several) built so exhibitors can build and rebuild their own stands inside it, show after show. Getting that open volume needs a long-span steel or space-frame roof, and getting power, water, compressed air and data to every exhibitor stand needs a grid of trenches or floor boxes built into the hall floor itself — both of which have to be right before the slab is poured or the roof erected, because retrofitting either is very costly. A rigging grid hung from the roof structure carries signage, lighting and AV for each show, and large-volume HVAC has to move and clear smoke across a very tall, open space. The programme is therefore driven first by the long-span roof and floor-service design, and at the back end by large-volume smoke-control proving, AV/rigging integration and a simulated load-in of a full show — not by the last coat of paint.

glossary.plain: a large open floor with no internal columns, made possible by long roof trusses or a space-frame.
service channels or recessed boxes cast into the hall floor that deliver power, water, compressed air and data up to each exhibitor stand.
a load-rated steel grid hung from the roof structure that signage, lighting and AV are hoisted from for each show.
large movable or operable partition walls that split one big hall into several smaller halls for concurrent, smaller events.
the heavy live-load capacity — often 30–50 kN/m² — the slab needs for exhibits, vehicles and forklifts.
engineered smoke-clearance (fans, vents, dampers) sized for a very tall, open hall rather than a normal room.
loading docks, marshalling yards and goods routes that move exhibit freight in and out of the halls.

must_get_right: The long-span roof (and the rigging grid it carries) gates almost everything else — sequence its design, procurement and erection first and protect it as the critical-path driver.
Floor-trench/floor-box service distribution and rigging-grid load points must be coordinated with the slab and roof design before pour and erection — retrofitting either is very costly.
Large-volume HVAC and smoke control need real, protected time for balancing and life-safety proving; this is not a normal fit-out item.
Prove hall subdivision, rigging/AV and back-of-house logistics together with a simulated exhibitor load-in/load-out before opening — that trial, not the last snag, is the true finish line.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. The long-span roof package is modelled as its own sub-network given its procurement lead time and erection-sequencing risk.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil, floor slab and roof erection run a 6-day week with roof-steel lift windows tied to crane availability; MEP rough-in and floor-trench works move to extended hours ahead of the life-safety test; commissioning runs against the availability of the first booked show and its load-in date.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs long-span roof procurement & erection → hall floor slab and floor-trench closure → MEP rough-in across the column-free volume → rigging grid and AV infrastructure → integrated life-safety and large-volume smoke-control test → simulated exhibitor load-in/load-out trial → handover. The roof and floor-service network, not the finishes, own the front and back of the programme.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen on hall floor-service layout and rigging-grid load points before the slab pours and the roof erects; authority approvals are obtained per phase gate; hall subdivision partition design is finalised before MEP rough-in; a single mobilisation.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule is roof-structure-led. The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Roof-steel erection needs dedicated large-crane windows and exclusion zones limiting other trades below. Floor-trench closure competes with slab-finishing crews for the same floor area, and back-of-house loading-dock access is shared across multiple concurrent trade deliveries late in the programme.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: long-span roof-steel fabrication/erection slippage, rigging-grid load-point rework where design and structure disagree, and smoke-control re-test loops. Schedule contingency is held immediately before the integrated life-safety test and before the load-in trial rather than spread thinly across finishing activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for roof erection, floor-trench closure and commissioning — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
